articles.label: Analysis
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 million budget gap: Where the cuts will land
articles.dek: With the new fiscal year starting tomorrow, county commissioners face hard choices on parks, libraries and road maintenance. A breakdown of what's on the chopping block.
brief: Escambia County faces a $47 million budget shortfall heading into fiscal year 2027, driven by declining property tax revenues and rising personnel costs.
Proposed cuts include reducing library hours by 30%, eliminating 12 parks maintenance positions and deferring $18 million in road resurfacing projects.
Commissioners will vote on the final budget tomorrow, with three of five members signaling support for the current proposal despite public opposition.
articles.body:
The Big Lagoon State Park access road hasn't been repaved since 2019. Potholes deep enough to swallow a bicycle tire dot the first quarter mile. County road crews patched it twice last year. They won't be back this year.

That stretch of asphalt sits on a list of 47 road projects Escambia County plans to defer indefinitely when the new fiscal year begins tomorrow. The county's $47 million budget gap—the largest in at least two decades—has forced commissioners into a round of cuts that will touch nearly every department and most residents.

Here's where the money isn't, and what that means for the county's 320,000 residents.

How the gap grew

Three factors converged to create the shortfall, according to budget documents presented at the June 12 commission workshop.

Property tax revenues came in $22 million below projections. The county had anticipated continued growth in taxable values following several years of rising home prices. Instead, values flattened as the housing market cooled, and successful appeals from commercial property owners—particularly along the Nine Mile Road corridor—reduced the tax base further.

Personnel costs rose $14 million, driven by contractual raises for sheriff's deputies and firefighters negotiated in 2024, plus a 12% increase in health insurance premiums.

The final $11 million came from the expiration of American Rescue Plan Act funds that had been plugging operational holes since 2022.

"We knew the ARPA money was temporary," said County Administrator Wes Moreno at the June 12 workshop. "What we didn't anticipate was the property tax shortfall hitting at the same time."

Libraries: Fewer hours, fewer staff

The Escambia County library system will absorb $3.2 million in cuts under the proposed budget. That translates to a 30% reduction in operating hours across all six branches.

The West Florida Public Library downtown will drop from 60 hours per week to 42. The Molino branch, which serves the northern end of the county, will operate just 20 hours weekly—down from 35.

Twelve full-time library positions will be eliminated through attrition and layoffs. The county has offered early retirement packages to five employees who qualify.

"We're essentially going back to pandemic-era hours," said Library Director Sandra Hutchins at a June 19 public hearing. "But without the pandemic-era excuse."

The cuts will end the library's homebound delivery program, which serves 340 residents who cannot travel to branches. Saturday children's programming will be eliminated at all locations except the downtown branch.

Parks: Maintenance deferred, positions cut

The parks department faces $4.1 million in reductions. Twelve maintenance positions—roughly one-third of the field staff—will be eliminated.

County documents outline what that means in practice: Mowing cycles at regional parks will extend from seven days to 14. Restroom cleaning at trailheads will drop from daily to three times weekly. Playground equipment inspections will shift from weekly to monthly.

Three boat ramps—at Bayview Park, Sanders Beach and Quintette—will lose their seasonal attendants. The ramps will remain open, but there will be no staff to assist with launches or monitor parking.

The county will also close the Brent Athletic Park swimming pool permanently. The pool requires $800,000 in repairs to its filtration system and deck. Those repairs are no longer in the budget.

"That pool has served this community for 40 years," said Tanyard resident Marcus Williams at the June 19 hearing. "You're telling my grandkids they can't learn to swim because you can't find $800,000?"

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Brent, said the decision was painful but unavoidable. "We can repair the pool or we can keep the Molino library open," he said. "We cannot do both."

Roads: $18 million in deferrals

The road maintenance budget will shrink by $8.7 million. But the real impact shows up in the capital projects list.

The county had planned to resurface 23 miles of roads in fiscal year 2027. That number drops to 11 miles under the proposed budget. Eighteen million dollars in resurfacing projects will be pushed to fiscal year 2028 or beyond—assuming revenues recover.

Among the deferred projects: Nine Mile Road from University Parkway to Pine Forest Road, a stretch that carries 35,000 vehicles daily. The road's surface rating dropped to "poor" in the county's 2025 assessment. It will stay that way.

Also deferred: Resurfacing of Mobile Highway from the state line to Navy Boulevard, and reconstruction of Old Corry Field Road near the county's animal shelter.

County Engineer Frank Nall said the deferrals will cost more in the long run. "Every year we delay, the repair costs increase roughly 7%," he told commissioners. "We're not saving money. We're borrowing against the future."

What's not being cut

Public safety accounts for 58% of the county's general fund budget. That share will grow to 61% under the proposed plan.

The Escambia County Sheriff's Office budget increases by $4.3 million, covering contractual raises and the addition of eight deputies assigned to the new Beulah substation. Fire-rescue adds $2.1 million for contractual raises and equipment replacement.

Commissioner Steven Barry, who chairs the budget committee, defended the public safety spending at the June 12 workshop. "We can debate library hours," he said. "We cannot debate response times when someone calls 911."

The county will also maintain full funding for the health department, emergency management and the elections office.

The politics of the vote

Tomorrow's budget vote appears likely to follow a familiar 3-2 split. Commissioners Barry, Bergosh and Mike Kohler have signaled support for the proposal as written. Commissioners Lumon May and Ander Crenshaw have pushed for alternatives.

May proposed a 0.25-mill property tax increase at the June 19 hearing. The increase would generate approximately $12 million annually—enough to restore library hours and avoid the parks layoffs. The proposal failed 3-2.

"We're asking residents to accept worse services while refusing to ask for a modest contribution," May said after the vote. "A quarter mill is $25 a year on a $100,000 home."

Kohler responded that any tax increase was off the table. "We made a commitment to hold the line," he said. "Residents are already stretched thin."

Crenshaw has proposed using $8 million from the county's reserve fund to soften the cuts. That proposal will come up for a vote tomorrow alongside the budget itself. It is expected to fail.

What happens next

The commission meets at 5:30 p.m. tomorrow in the Ernie Lee Magaha Government Building. The budget vote requires a simple majority.

If approved, the cuts take effect immediately. Library schedules change Thursday. Parks staff reductions begin with the first pay period in July. Road projects already underway will continue; deferred projects will not start.

The county's next budget cycle begins in April 2027. Whether revenues recover enough to restore services depends on factors largely outside the commission's control: property values, insurance costs, state funding formulas.

Moreno, the county administrator, offered a measured assessment at the June 12 workshop. "This budget reflects our current reality," he said. "It's not the budget any of us wanted. It's the budget we have."

The Big Lagoon access road will wait.

articles.label: Downtown
articles.headline: The Palafox Street vacancy problem isn't going away
articles.dek: Six months after the downtown master plan promised a retail revival, storefronts sit empty and landlords aren't budging on rent. What's really blocking recovery.
brief: At least 14 ground-floor retail spaces on Palafox Street between Main and Garden sit vacant, roughly the same count as when the Downtown Master Plan passed in January.
Commercial landlords are holding asking rents at $28-35 per square foot despite vacancies, citing property tax increases and investor expectations.
City incentive programs launched this spring have produced zero signed leases, and small business owners say the application process takes too long to matter.
articles.body:
The sandwich board outside 21 Palafox Place advertises a business that closed eight months ago. Wind has scraped the vinyl lettering down to ghosts. Somebody taped a handwritten "For Lease" sign in the window, but the phone number's been disconnected since March.

Walk three blocks north and count the gaps. The old guitar shop. The boutique with the turquoise door. The frozen yogurt place that made it two summers. Between Main Street and Garden Street, at least 14 ground-floor retail spaces sit empty. A few have broker signs. Most just have dark windows and dust settling on the sills.

This wasn't supposed to be the story six months after the city adopted its Downtown Master Plan.

The promise and the problem

In January, Pensacola City Council voted 6-1 to adopt a 94-page master plan that called downtown "the economic and cultural heart of the region." The plan promised a retail revival. Streetscape investments. A coordinated strategy to fill vacant storefronts and attract the kind of local businesses that make people walk instead of drive.

Six months later, the vacancy count hasn't moved. If anything, it's gotten worse. The Mediterranean restaurant at Palafox and Intendencia closed in April. The vintage clothing store next to the old Saenger lasted until May.

"We've had exactly zero net new retail openings on Palafox this calendar year," said Marcus Webb, executive director of the Downtown Improvement Board. "Zero."

Webb sat in his office on the second floor of the Blount Building, a stack of broker listings on his desk. He's been tracking the numbers since 2019. The vacancy rate for ground-floor retail in the Palafox core hit 23 percent in his latest count. Pre-pandemic, it was 11 percent.

"I can show you the spreadsheet," he said. "But you can also just walk outside."

The rent question

Ask anyone in local retail why storefronts stay empty, and you'll hear the same word within thirty seconds. Rent.

Commercial asking rates on Palafox currently range from $28 to $35 per square foot, according to listings reviewed by The Flightline. A 1,500-square-foot space at the low end runs $3,500 a month before utilities, insurance, or buildout costs. At the high end, it's $4,375.

For comparison: similar-sized retail space in downtown Mobile, Alabama, lists between $18 and $24 per square foot. In Tallahassee's College Town district, rates hover around $22.

Pensacola landlords say the numbers reflect reality.

"My property taxes went up 19 percent in two years," said Gene Kirkland, who owns three commercial buildings on South Palafox. "Insurance is up 40 percent since 2022. I'm not being greedy. I'm trying to break even."

Kirkland has one vacant unit, a corner space that's been empty since a coffee shop left in 2024. He said he's had inquiries but no serious offers. The prospective tenants who come through want rents in the low twenties. He can't make those numbers work.

"I'd rather sit empty than sign a lease that puts me underwater," he said.

Other landlords have less direct relationships with their properties. At least four Palafox buildings are owned by out-of-state investment groups, according to Escambia County property records. Calls and emails to those entities were not returned.

Webb, at the Downtown Improvement Board, said absentee ownership complicates negotiations.

"You're not dealing with Gene Kirkland, who lives here and walks past his own building every day," he said. "You're dealing with a property manager in Atlanta who's got 30 other assets in their portfolio. Pensacola's just a line item. They're not going to cut rent because it makes the street look better."

The incentive gap

The city tried to address the problem. In March, Mayor D.C. Reeves announced two new programs aimed at filling storefronts: a $50,000 buildout grant fund for new retail tenants and a six-month rent subsidy pilot that would cover up to $1,500 monthly for qualifying small businesses.

"We're putting our money where our mouth is," Reeves said at the time. "We want local entrepreneurs to know that Pensacola is open for business."

Three months later, both programs have produced zero signed leases.

The buildout grant fund received 11 applications. None have been approved. According to city spokesperson Dana Chen, the review process requires applicants to submit architectural plans, proof of lease negotiations, and a three-year financial projection. Average processing time is running 14 weeks.

"By the time they'd approve me, I'd have given up and found a different space," said Reena Patel, who applied in April for a grant to open a spice shop. She's now negotiating for a location in East Hill instead. "I can't wait four months to find out if I'm getting $8,000."

The rent subsidy pilot has a different problem. It's capped at businesses with fewer than five employees and gross revenues under $250,000. That eliminates most of the restaurant and bar operators who might otherwise anchor a block.

"The people who can actually afford Palafox rent don't qualify," said Webb. "And the people who qualify can't afford Palafox rent even with the subsidy. It's a circle."

Chen said the city is reviewing feedback and may adjust program requirements before the next fiscal year.

What's working, what's not

Not every downtown block looks like Palafox.

South Jefferson Street, two blocks east, has three new businesses this year: a ceramics studio, a barber shop, and a wine bar. The difference, according to tenants, is rent. Spaces on Jefferson run $16 to $22 per square foot.

"I looked at Palafox first," said David Ngo, who opened Jefferson Street Provisions, a wine and cheese shop, in February. "Loved the foot traffic. But I'd have needed to charge $25 for a cheese plate to make it work. That's not my business."

Ngo's paying $2,100 a month for 1,100 square feet. He said he turned profitable in April. On Palafox, at the higher end of the rent range, the same space would cost closer to $3,200.

The other model that's working: restaurants with liquor licenses and weekend late-night traffic. Establishments that can charge $15 cocktails and pack 200 people on a Saturday can absorb Palafox rents. The Bodega on South Palafox, which opened last fall, is an example. So is The District, a few blocks north.

But the retail spaces—the boutiques, the bookstores, the gift shops—those are the gaps. And those gaps change how downtown feels.

"You can have great restaurants, but if there's nothing to do during the day, people don't come downtown," said Webb. "They come for dinner and they leave. That's not a neighborhood. That's a food court."

The landlord standoff

The question underneath all the numbers is whether downtown Pensacola has a market-rate problem or a landlord-behavior problem. Put another way: are rents too high, or are they exactly where the market sets them?

Economics would suggest that persistent vacancies should drive rents down. If no one's leasing at $32 a square foot, the price should fall until someone does.

But that's not what's happening.

Commercial real estate brokers who spoke with The Flightline pointed to several factors that keep landlords holding firm.

First, many owners bought or refinanced during the low-interest-rate era of 2020-2021. Their debt service—the monthly mortgage payment—is based on assumptions about what the property could generate. Cutting rent means the building doesn't cash-flow, even if it's occupied.

Second, property values are based partly on lease rates. If an owner signs a below-market lease, the building's appraised value drops. For owners who plan to sell or refinance, that's a problem.

Third, some landlords are simply waiting. They believe downtown Pensacola is on an upward trajectory—that the waterfront development, the new hotels, the momentum will eventually bring tenants who can pay. Better to hold out than to lock in a five-year lease at a discount.

"It's a bet," said commercial broker Shelly Morton, who's worked Pensacola properties for two decades. "They're betting that downtown is going to pop and they'll look smart for waiting. But in the meantime, the street looks dead. And that makes the pop less likely."

What the city can do

City Council's options are limited. Pensacola can't force landlords to lower rent. It can't compel property owners to accept tenants.

Some cities have tried vacancy taxes—fees assessed on properties that sit empty for extended periods. San Francisco has one. So does Washington, D.C. The theory is that the tax changes the calculus, making it more expensive to hold out for a dream tenant than to sign a lease now.

When asked about a vacancy tax at a June council meeting, Mayor Reeves called it "something we're monitoring but not actively pursuing." Council member Teniadé Broughton said she'd requested a staff analysis but hadn't received one.

Other options include zoning changes that allow residential on ground floors—currently prohibited in much of the Palafox corridor—or expanded historic tax credits to offset buildout costs. None are currently before the council.

Webb, at the Downtown Improvement Board, said the city's biggest lever is attention.

"When the mayor talks about something every week, it moves," he said. "When it fades off the agenda, nothing happens. Right now, downtown vacancy is not a priority. It's in the plan, but it's not in the conversation."

What's next

Summer is the slow season. The tourists are at the beach. The college students are gone. Retail traffic on Palafox drops by roughly a third between Memorial Day and Labor Day, according to DIB foot-traffic counters.

The test will come in the fall. If the master plan's promises mean anything, the next six months should show progress: new tenants, filled storefronts, a sense that the gaps are closing.

The alternative is that Palafox becomes what some stretches already feel like—a place to walk past rather than walk to. A street of restaurants bookended by dark windows. A downtown that's busiest at 9 p.m. and quietest at noon.

For now, the sandwich board outside 21 Palafox Place is still there. The vinyl is still peeling. And the phone number on the "For Lease" sign is still disconnected.

Someone should probably take that down.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's new flight training contract could reshape the local economy
articles.dek: A $200 million deal with a Texas-based defense contractor means more jobs but raises questions about who benefits when the base expands.
brief: Department of Defense awards $200 million contract to Valkyrie Defense Solutions for expanded flight training operations at NAS Pensacola
Deal expected to create 450 direct jobs and relocate up to 200 contractor employees to the Pensacola area over 18 months
Local officials and housing advocates split on whether existing infrastructure can absorb the growth
articles.body:
The hangars at Sherman Field sit quiet most afternoons now. By this time next year, they won't.

The Department of Defense announced Thursday that Valkyrie Defense Solutions, a Fort Worth-based aerospace contractor, will take over and expand primary flight training operations at Naval Air Station Pensacola under a five-year, $200 million contract. The deal marks the largest single defense procurement tied to the base in more than a decade.

For a region where the military accounts for roughly one in five jobs, the contract represents something close to an economic event horizon. More money. More people. More demand for housing, childcare, restaurant seats and roads that already strain under summer tourist traffic.

"This is exactly the kind of investment we've been working toward," Escambia County Commission Chair David Reynolds said at a Friday morning press conference outside the county administrative building. "Pensacola is proving once again that we're the cradle of naval aviation."

What he didn't mention: the county has no formal plan for absorbing the growth.

The deal

Valkyrie Defense Solutions will assume responsibility for the Training Air Wing Six undergraduate flight training program beginning in January 2027. The contract covers aircraft maintenance, ground-based instruction and simulator operations for approximately 1,200 student naval aviators per year.

Company officials said they expect to hire 450 workers locally over the next 18 months, with starting wages averaging $58,000 for maintenance technicians and $72,000 for certified flight instructors. Another 150 to 200 employees will relocate from the company's existing facilities in Texas and Florida's Space Coast.

"Pensacola has the workforce, the weather and the institutional knowledge," said Maria Castellanos, Valkyrie's vice president of government programs, during a call with reporters. "We're not coming in to change what works. We're coming in to add capacity."

The contract replaces a previous arrangement with L3Harris Technologies, which had managed portions of the training pipeline since 2019. A spokesperson for L3Harris declined to comment on the transition.

Housing math

The new jobs arrive in a housing market already running hot.

Median home prices in Escambia County have risen 34% since 2021, according to data from the Pensacola Association of Realtors. Rental vacancy rates hover near 4%—well below the 6% threshold economists consider healthy. A two-bedroom apartment in the Cordova Park area now averages $1,450 per month, up from $1,100 three years ago.

Adding 600-plus households to that market in 18 months presents what housing advocate Rachel Simmons calls "a math problem with no good answer."

Simmons directs the Pensacola Housing Coalition, a nonprofit that tracks affordability trends and advocates for low-income renters. She said the Valkyrie contract will accelerate displacement already underway in neighborhoods like Brownsville and Tanyard, where longtime residents compete with newcomers for a shrinking supply of affordable units.

"Every time the base expands, we hear about jobs and economic impact," Simmons said. "We don't hear about the family that gets priced out of their rental because a contractor employee can pay more."

County officials point to several apartment complexes under construction along Mobile Highway and Nine Mile Road as evidence the market is responding. Building permits for multifamily units are up 22% over last year.

But most of those projects target renters earning $50,000 or more—roughly the median income for Valkyrie's incoming workforce, not for the service workers who cook their food and clean their offices.

Infrastructure questions

Traffic engineers have their own concerns.

Navy Boulevard, the main artery connecting NAS Pensacola to the rest of the city, already operates at or near capacity during shift changes. The Florida Department of Transportation rated a two-mile stretch between Barrancas Avenue and Main Street as "failing" in its most recent corridor assessment.

A planned widening project remains stuck in the design phase, with construction not expected to begin until 2029 at the earliest. Escambia County Public Works Director James Thornton said the Valkyrie contract "doesn't change our timeline, but it does raise the stakes."

"We're going to have more cars on roads that were designed for a different era," Thornton said. "There's no way around that in the short term."

The base itself will handle most of the growth internally. NAS Pensacola Commanding Officer Capt. Jennifer Walsh said in a statement that existing hangar space and classroom facilities can accommodate the expanded training program without major construction. Valkyrie will lease approximately 40,000 square feet of additional office space off-base, likely in the industrial parks along Navy Boulevard.

Who benefits

FloridaWest Economic Development Council, the public-private partnership that recruited Valkyrie, estimates the contract will generate $312 million in annual economic impact once fully operational. That figure includes direct wages, supply chain spending and what economists call "induced effects"—the multiplier created when new workers spend money at local businesses.

The methodology behind such projections often draws skepticism from academics. But even conservative estimates suggest the Pensacola metro area will see meaningful job growth in sectors beyond aerospace.

"You're talking about restaurants, car dealerships, pediatricians, daycare centers," said Scott Luth, FloridaWest's CEO. "The ripple effects are real."

Less clear is whether those ripples reach everyone.

Valkyrie has committed to hiring locally for at least 70% of its new positions, a pledge Luth called "unprecedented" for a defense contractor of its size. The company will partner with Pensacola State College to create a fast-track aviation maintenance certification program, with the first cohort of 60 students beginning this fall.

But the jobs that pay $58,000 require specific technical credentials. The jobs that don't—janitorial services, food service, grounds maintenance—typically go to subcontractors who set their own wage scales. Valkyrie declined to say whether it would require subcontractors to meet minimum pay standards.

History echoes

Pensacola has absorbed military expansions before. The base's footprint has grown and contracted with the tides of American defense policy since 1914, when the Navy established its first aviation training facility on the shores of Pensacola Bay.

Old-timers remember the boom years of the 1980s, when Reagan-era defense spending swelled the base population and transformed the surrounding neighborhoods. They also remember the hangover of the 1990s drawdowns, when the end of the Cold War left empty storefronts along Palafox Street.

"The base giveth and the base taketh away," said former City Council member Sam Jenkins, who represented District 6 from 1998 to 2006. "Smart communities figure out how to catch the good years without getting wiped out in the bad ones."

Current Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves has proposed creating a "base impact fund"—a dedicated reserve account that would collect a portion of new tax revenue generated by military-related growth. The money would support affordable housing development and infrastructure improvements in neighborhoods most affected by expansion.

The proposal requires City Council approval. It has not yet been scheduled for a vote.

For now, the hangars at Sherman Field wait. The contract is signed. The jobs are coming. The only question left is who will be ready to catch them.
